A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TimeDART study. All 19 pages, including Appendices A–F, are available and readable; text, equations, tables and figures support a complete comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original forecasting comparisons, component ablations, sensitivity experiments and prediction examples in Section 4 and Appendices C–F.

after.justification: v2 retains these original empirical results, including forecasting benchmarks and supplementary experiments.

M1.justification: Section 3 and Figure 1 retain the same patching, causal Transformer encoder, diffusion process, masked denoising decoder, optimization objective and downstream fine-tuning procedure.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same eight datasets: four ETT datasets, Electricity, Traffic, Weather and Exchange. The in-domain setting and mixed pre-training across five energy datasets are unchanged.

E2.justification: Table 2 retains SimMTM, self-supervised PatchTST, TimeMAE, CoST, supervised PatchTST, DLinear and random initialization. Comparator membership in the cross-domain comparisons and forecasting visualizations is also unchanged.

E3.justification: Section 4.1 and Appendix A retain the chronological splits, 336-step look-back window, prediction horizons of 96/192/336/720, MSE/MAE metrics, training budgets and model settings. The numerical corrections do not establish any protocol change.

E4.justification: The same component ablations, noise-step/scheduler sensitivity tests, decoder-depth and patch-length sweeps, and forecasting case studies remain. Their designs and per-horizon evidence are unchanged; the differences concern corrected numerical summaries.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. Tables retain point estimates and averages across four forecast horizons; correcting those averages does not change the reporting practice.

E6.justification: Table 5 corrects ETTm2 linear-scheduler MSE from 0.369 to 0.269. Table 9 replaces both erroneous Avg. rows, previously duplicating ETTh2's 720-step values, with correct four-horizon means. For example, cosine MSE/MAE becomes 0.345/0.386 for ETTh2 and 0.257/0.316 for ETTm2, previously 0.390/0.425 for both. Per-horizon results remain unchanged. Table 2's 0.33-to-0.330 edit is numerically equivalent.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, diffusion equations, autoregressive formulation and optimization objective in Section 3 are unchanged, as is the ELBO derivation in Appendix B.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same contributions: integrating diffusion with autoregressive modeling, capturing global and local features, and achieving state-of-the-art forecasting performance.

C2.justification: Interpretations of component importance, scheduler smoothness, decoder capacity and patch length are unchanged. The discussion of Exchange overfitting and computational tradeoffs is also retained without new qualifications.

D1.justification: Appendix A retains the same implementation, optimizer, learning-rate choices, batch sizes, training epochs, representation dimensions and hardware statement. The code-access statement and link are unchanged.

R1.justification: The cited works, reference list and related-work discussion are unchanged, with no revision to TimeDART's positioning relative to earlier approaches.

P1.justification: The running header changes from 'Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2025' to 'Preprint'. Body prose, section order and appendix organization remain unchanged.

P2.justification: Table 5 moves from page 10 in v1 to page 9 in v2, accompanied by local spacing and page-flow changes. Figure 2 shifts within page 10. All figures and tables are retained, without figure redrawing or substantial display restructuring.

improvement.justification: v2 improves reporting accuracy by correcting Table 5's ETTm2 linear-scheduler MSE and making Table 9's averages agree with the unchanged per-horizon results and main-text summaries. This resolves concrete internal inconsistencies in the sensitivity evidence. The gain is limited because the method, experimental coverage, primary results and interpretations remain unchanged.
